passages: Home - Cryptocurrency News - House Crypto Tax Bill Proposes $10 Fee Relief and New Wash-Sale Rules

The House crypto tax bill proposes relief for network and transaction fees under $10 while extending wash-sale rules to digital assets. H.R. 10357 will face a Sept. 16 Ways and Means Committee markup as lawmakers debate broader changes to federal crypto taxation.

House lawmakers unveiled a 114-page crypto tax bill on Sept. 15. It offers relief for small network fees and expands wash-sale rules. The Ways and Means Committee will consider it at its Sept. 16 markup.

Committee Chair Jason Smith unveiled the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act following the drafting of two separate proposals. According to Bloomberg Government, the Republican from Missouri released the draft package on Monday evening. The draft contains proposals related to taxes on transactions, gains, losses, transfers, mining, staking, wash sales, and brokers.
Also Read: Fin.com Raises $20M as Stablecoin Payments Expansion Accelerates

One provision seeks to reduce tax on transactions and network fees of less than $10. This provision seeks to address the issue of small blockchain transactions that give rise to tax-reporting obligations under existing tax laws. The exemption applies to persons who made over 5,000 transactions in the past year.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 A new U.S. House crypto tax bill proposes making blockchain network fees under $10 tax-exempt. The 114-page proposal also covers staking, mining, wash-sale rules, transfers and digital asset gains and losses. pic.twitter.com/xrDZjPdI55

A small fee allowance would primarily benefit low-volume users engaged in regular transactions involving digital assets. The measure would be used to lower the reporting in regard to low blockchain costs. High-volume users will not qualify for the carve-out under the 5,000-transfers threshold.

Smaller transactions had been discussed by Congress during its consideration of the House tax bill. Members of Congress were already contemplating the reduction of reporting obligations of digital asset users back in June. Mining, staking, and other common operations were also discussed at that time.

Broker reporting was also becoming more comprehensive under federal legislation. IRS rules required tracking on a wallet-by-wallet basis, and broker reporting of gross proceeds became mandatory on Form 1099-DA starting from 2025. Phased-in cost basis reporting would apply to transactions conducted in 2026.

Coinbase advocated for the relief of small payments during the prior discussion in the House. In testimony at a Ways and Means hearing on June 9, Coinbase Vice President of Tax Lawrence Zlatkin said that stablecoin payments and blockchain fees entail a significant burden. Coinbase also advocated for delayed tax treatment of mining and staking rewards.

Under the crypto tax bill, wash sale rules will apply to digital assets. Federal wash sale rules currently apply restrictions on the recognition of loss if the taxpayers repurchase substantially similar securities shortly after the loss has been claimed. Digital assets are not currently included under the statutory rule.

The inclusion of such a rule originates from H.R. 9172, known as the Applying Existing Tax Anti-Abuse Rules to Digital Assets Act. Representatives Jodey Arrington and Mike Carey had introduced the act in June. Qualified US dollar stablecoins were exempted from the rule on wash sale.

The wash sale rule is expected to generate revenue amounting to $2.074 billion from 2026 to 2036. It is believed that existing rules should adapt to changes in financial technology. According to Smith, taxpayers need some standardization for digital assets.

Earlier proposal by the House regarding changing the timing of taxes related to mining and staking. H.R. 9175, or the Tax Clarity for Mining and Staking Act, would allow the taxpayers to defer the income recognition if there is a sale of the newly minted tokens.
It was estimated that this would result in a loss of federal revenue amounting to $2.956 billion between fiscal years 2026 and 2036.

Currently, the staking rewards are treated as ordinary income once the taxpayer obtains dominion and control. Its value during that period becomes the cost basis of any future gain or loss of the asset. Industry associations have called on the lawmakers to defer the taxation upon a sale of staking rewards.
The Blockchain Association, Crypto Council for Innovation, and Digital Chamber opposed the limit of five years to deferred taxation. They have urged Congress to adopt H.R. 9175 without changes.
The banking organizations stated that delayed taxation could provide a crypto reward tax treatment different from interest, dividends, and other income types of investments.
As reported by Punchbowl News on Sept. 13, the Republicans in the Ways and Means Committee were considering removing the mining and staking timing provision from the legislation package.
Sources familiar with the negotiations called it a major point of contention with Horsford. The final committee debate will show whether lawmakers retain, revise, or remove those provisions.

In terms of the crypto tax bill, the September 16 markup comes after a Ways and Means hearing held on June 9 on multiple digital asset tax measures, which involved Coinbase, Fidelity Investments, Coin Center, and New York University’s Tax Law Center.
The hearing covered various topics such as mining, staking, charitable contributions, voluntary disclosures, wash sales, and more tax-related matters.

The September 16 markup will be the next official proceeding in the passage of H.R. 10357. Committee members can discuss the bill text, propose amendments, and vote on advancing it. Passing of the tax package will take it a step closer to becoming a law, while rejection will put it at risk of further delays.

It is not the only legislative action taking place on crypto this week in Washington. The Senate plans to make a procedural vote on the CLARITY Act on September 15; 60 votes will be necessary to advance the market structure measure. While these legislative packages target different parts of the crypto federal policy.

The crypto tax bill will be considered by the Ways and Means Committee together with the EFIN Verification Act of 2026, H.R. 10334, and five other bills. These other bills deal with healthcare and cobalt mining and some other policy areas. The markup will define the future of the crypto tax bill.

Lawmakers managed to incorporate several tax proposals into one package. Now the crypto tax bill covers small fee relief, anti-abuse provisions, broker reporting requirements, and several digital asset tax matters. The September 16 markup will show what happens to the package of the crypto tax bill in the House.

The House crypto tax bill proposes relief for network and transaction fees under $10 while extending wash-sale rules to digital assets. H.R. 10357 will face a Sept. 16 Ways and Means Committee markup as lawmakers debate broader changes to federal crypto taxation.

House lawmakers unveiled a 114-page crypto tax bill on Sept. 15. It offers relief for small network fees and expands wash-sale rules. The Ways and Means Committee will consider it at its Sept. 16 markup.

Committee Chair Jason Smith unveiled the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act following the drafting of two separate proposals. According to Bloomberg Government, the Republican from Missouri released the draft package on Monday evening. The draft contains proposals related to taxes on transactions, gains, losses, transfers, mining, staking, wash sales, and brokers.
Also Read: Fin.com Raises $20M as Stablecoin Payments Expansion Accelerates

One provision seeks to reduce tax on transactions and network fees of less than $10. This provision seeks to address the issue of small blockchain transactions that give rise to tax-reporting obligations under existing tax laws. The exemption applies to persons who made over 5,000 transactions in the past year.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 A new U.S. House crypto tax bill proposes making blockchain network fees under $10 tax-exempt. The 114-page proposal also covers staking, mining, wash-sale rules, transfers and digital asset gains and losses. pic.twitter.com/xrDZjPdI55

A small fee allowance would primarily benefit low-volume users engaged in regular transactions involving digital assets. The measure would be used to lower the reporting in regard to low blockchain costs. High-volume users will not qualify for the carve-out under the 5,000-transfers threshold.

Smaller transactions had been discussed by Congress during its consideration of the House tax bill. Members of Congress were already contemplating the reduction of reporting obligations of digital asset users back in June. Mining, staking, and other common operations were also discussed at that time.

Broker reporting was also becoming more comprehensive under federal legislation. IRS rules required tracking on a wallet-by-wallet basis, and broker reporting of gross proceeds became mandatory on Form 1099-DA starting from 2025. Phased-in cost basis reporting would apply to transactions conducted in 2026.

Coinbase advocated for the relief of small payments during the prior discussion in the House. In testimony at a Ways and Means hearing on June 9, Coinbase Vice President of Tax Lawrence Zlatkin said that stablecoin payments and blockchain fees entail a significant burden. Coinbase also advocated for delayed tax treatment of mining and staking rewards.

Under the crypto tax bill, wash sale rules will apply to digital assets. Federal wash sale rules currently apply restrictions on the recognition of loss if the taxpayers repurchase substantially similar securities shortly after the loss has been claimed. Digital assets are not currently included under the statutory rule.

The inclusion of such a rule originates from H.R. 9172, known as the Applying Existing Tax Anti-Abuse Rules to Digital Assets Act. Representatives Jodey Arrington and Mike Carey had introduced the act in June. Qualified US dollar stablecoins were exempted from the rule on wash sale.

The wash sale rule is expected to generate revenue amounting to $2.074 billion from 2026 to 2036. It is believed that existing rules should adapt to changes in financial technology. According to Smith, taxpayers need some standardization for digital assets.

Earlier proposal by the House regarding changing the timing of taxes related to mining and staking. H.R. 9175, or the Tax Clarity for Mining and Staking Act, would allow the taxpayers to defer the income recognition if there is a sale of the newly minted tokens.
It was estimated that this would result in a loss of federal revenue amounting to $2.956 billion between fiscal years 2026 and 2036.

Currently, the staking rewards are treated as ordinary income once the taxpayer obtains dominion and control. Its value during that period becomes the cost basis of any future gain or loss of the asset. Industry associations have called on the lawmakers to defer the taxation upon a sale of staking rewards.
The Blockchain Association, Crypto Council for Innovation, and Digital Chamber opposed the limit of five years to deferred taxation. They have urged Congress to adopt H.R. 9175 without changes.
The banking organizations stated that delayed taxation could provide a crypto reward tax treatment different from interest, dividends, and other income types of investments.
As reported by Punchbowl News on Sept. 13, the Republicans in the Ways and Means Committee were considering removing the mining and staking timing provision from the legislation package.
Sources familiar with the negotiations called it a major point of contention with Horsford. The final committee debate will show whether lawmakers retain, revise, or remove those provisions.

In terms of the crypto tax bill, the September 16 markup comes after a Ways and Means hearing held on June 9 on multiple digital asset tax measures, which involved Coinbase, Fidelity Investments, Coin Center, and New York University’s Tax Law Center.
The hearing covered various topics such as mining, staking, charitable contributions, voluntary disclosures, wash sales, and more tax-related matters.

The September 16 markup will be the next official proceeding in the passage of H.R. 10357. Committee members can discuss the bill text, propose amendments, and vote on advancing it. Passing of the tax package will take it a step closer to becoming a law, while rejection will put it at risk of further delays.

It is not the only legislative action taking place on crypto this week in Washington. The Senate plans to make a procedural vote on the CLARITY Act on September 15; 60 votes will be necessary to advance the market structure measure. While these legislative packages target different parts of the crypto federal policy.

The crypto tax bill will be considered by the Ways and Means Committee together with the EFIN Verification Act of 2026, H.R. 10334, and five other bills. These other bills deal with healthcare and cobalt mining and some other policy areas. The markup will define the future of the crypto tax bill.

Lawmakers managed to incorporate several tax proposals into one package. Now the crypto tax bill covers small fee relief, anti-abuse provisions, broker reporting requirements, and several digital asset tax matters. The September 16 markup will show what happens to the package of the crypto tax bill in the House.

candidate.title: Turkey’s strategic duality. Building a security architecture beyond NATO - New Eastern Europe

sources.title: RIAC :: The Ankara NATO Summit: Turkey’s Capacity to Manage the Duality within the Western Security Architecture - Российский совет по международным делам
passages: The NATO Summit to be held in Ankara in 2026 represents a critical meeting that will reopen the debate on Turkey’s position within the Alliance.
This summit should not be regarded merely as one of NATO’s routine diplomatic meetings that sets the Alliance’s agenda.

Indeed, this historical context demonstrates that Turkey is emerging not only as the host country, but also as a central actor capable of reading the eastern and southern axes of the European security order simultaneously.

While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns.
The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question.
Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges.

At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms.
During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank.
However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century.
This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy.
Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency.
The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era.
Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers.

Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice.
In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas.

From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale.
Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible.

By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way.

extraction.body: The NATO Summit to be held in Ankara in 2026 represents a critical meeting that will reopen the debate on Turkey’s position within the Alliance. This summit should not be regarded merely as one of NATO’s routine diplomatic meetings that sets the Alliance’s agenda. It will also serve as a platform through which Turkey’s place in the Western security architecture, its strategic weight within the Alliance, and its multidimensional foreign policy capacity will become more visible amid the fragile security perceptions currently shaping the West. For this reason, the summit to be held in Ankara on 7–8 July 2026 will, in a sense, also constitute a moment of self-questioning for the Western security alliance. Indeed, this historical context demonstrates that Turkey is emerging not only as the host country, but also as a central actor capable of reading the eastern and southern axes of the European security order simultaneously. The most significant meaning of the Ankara Summit for Turkey lies in the fact that Turkey’s position within NATO can no longer be explained solely through geographical advantage, military capacity, or historical membership. During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank. However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century. Turkey is no longer merely a security buffer located on the margins of the Alliance; rather, it has become a constitutive security actor situated at the intersection of the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Balkans, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and critical energy transit routes. In this respect, the Ankara Summit provides an important platform for discussing Turkey’s evolving position beyond its traditional role within NATO. Turkey’s position within NATO has increasingly been redefined through its defense industry capacity. The country is no longer merely a state that uses NATO weapons systems or contributes to the Alliance’s military planning because of its geographical location. Through its growing capabilities in unmanned aerial vehicles, land systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, air defense systems and ammunition production, Turkey has become an actor that strengthens its own defense production infrastructure within the Alliance and transforms this capacity into an instrument of foreign policy. This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy. Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency. Instead, it does so by developing its national capabilities, becoming a producing actor in the defense industry, therefore prioritizing its own security concerns when necessary. This gives Turkey a new bargaining space within NATO and moves Ankara’s position in the Alliance onto a more autonomous, flexible and multidimensional ground. Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges. European countries need Turkey’s military capacity, geographical position, role in migration management, and influence over the Black Sea, Caucasus, etc. At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms. This contradiction constitutes one of the most important structural problems behind the Ankara NATO Summit. Turkey is indispensable for European security, yet its institutional place within the European security architecture remains contested and insufficiently defined. For this reason, the Ankara Summit will not merely mean that Turkey is hosting NATO. It will also provide Turkey with an opportunity to present its own security agenda to the Alliance, to reveal the narrowing of Europe’s security understanding, and to underline the necessity of evaluating multidimensional crisis areas together. In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas. From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale. At this point, Turkey’s significance stems not only from its proximity to crisis regions, but also from its ability to read these crises simultaneously and to understand the connections between them. Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible. By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way. Therefore, the Ankara Summit is not only a security meeting; it is also a reflection of changing hegemonic relations in the global system, internal tensions within the Western alliance, and Turkey’s capacity to grasp this transformation. The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era. Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers. Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice. Ankara’s defense industry breakthrough, multidimensional diplomacy, direct engagement with crisis regions and more autonomous position within NATO show that Turkey is not passively observing changing global power balances. Rather, it is trying to open its own space within this transformation. The Ankara NATO Summit demonstrates that Turkey has moved beyond its traditional position within NATO and has become a strategic actor capable of managing the duality within the Western security architecture. While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns. In this regard, the fundamental question of the Ankara Summit is the following: will NATO and Europe continue to see Turkey merely as a military capacity and geographical advantage needed in times of crisis, or will they recognize Turkey as a constitutive, transformative and strategic actor in the reconstruction of the European security architecture? The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question. For this reason, the Ankara Summit will not merely mean that Turkey is hosting NATO. It will also provide Turkey with an opportunity to present its own security agenda to the Alliance, to reveal the narrowing of Europe’s security understanding, and to underline the necessity of evaluating multidimensional crisis areas together. In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas. From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale.

At this point, Turkey’s significance stems not only from its proximity to crisis regions, but also from its ability to read these crises simultaneously and to understand the connections between them. Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible. By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way. Therefore, the Ankara Summit is not only a security meeting; it is also a reflection of changing hegemonic relations in the global system, internal tensions within the Western alliance, and Turkey’s capacity to grasp this transformation.

The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era. Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers. Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice. Ankara’s defense industry breakthrough, multidimensional diplomacy, direct engagement with crisis regions and more autonomous position within NATO show that Turkey is not passively observing changing global power balances. Rather, it is trying to open its own space within this transformation.

The Ankara NATO Summit demonstrates that Turkey has moved beyond its traditional position within NATO and has become a strategic actor capable of managing the duality within the Western security architecture. While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns. In this regard, the fundamental question of the Ankara Summit is the following: will NATO and Europe continue to see Turkey merely as a military capacity and geographical advantage needed in times of crisis, or will they recognize Turkey as a constitutive, transformative and strategic actor in the reconstruction of the European security architecture? The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question.

extraction.body: The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. A new agreement with Middle East powers demonstrates just how Turkey is acquiring the ability to organize other states around its own security relationships. September 21, 2026 - Nikola Lunić - Articles and Commentary Turkey is not leaving NATO. The harder question is whether the Alliance can accommodate a member that is simultaneously building a security architecture of its own. The defence agreement signed in Mecca on August 7th by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan initially looked like another regional arrangement produced by a Middle East in turmoil. Its implications may extend well beyond the three signatories. The agreement declares that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described the mechanism as technically similar to NATO’s Article 5, while stressing that it is not directed against Iran or any other country. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has indicated that the framework could expand, with Egypt among the possible future participants. The significance of the agreement lies in what it reveals about Turkey’s evolving approach to power. Ankara has spent years pursuing greater strategic autonomy while remaining a member of the western alliance system. The Mecca agreement suggests that Ankara may now be moving towards something more ambitious: strategic duality, in which Turkey stays inside NATO while building security relationships outside it in which it can act as a leading power. That possibility deserves closer attention in Europe. Turkey’s acquisition of the Russian S-400 air defence system offers an instructive precedent. The dispute which erupted between Ankara and Washington was connected to a weapons purchase that the US judged incompatible with NATO’s security architecture and risky for the F-35 programme. Turkey was removed from the F-35 programme and faced sanctions in retaliation. The episode demonstrated that NATO membership does not give Ankara unlimited freedom to build capabilities that conflict with core Allied interests. The Mecca agreement, however, raises a different kind of issue. The S-400 could be kept outside a procurement programme, with its deployment restricted and its interoperability denied. A security commitment is harder to unwind. Once institutionalized through ministerial consultations, military planning, intelligence cooperation and expectations of mutual support, such a commitment acquires political momentum on its own. The Mecca framework, though still deliberately flexible, is already moving in that direction. The question for NATO concerns the point at which external partnerships develop into a second collective-security framework. That distinction may not matter today. It could matter enormously in a future crisis. The Mecca agreement did not create a security network from nothing. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already concluded a strategic mutual-defence agreement in September 2025, under which aggression against one would be regarded as aggression against both. Turkey and Pakistan have spent years deepening a defence relationship covering industry, technology and counterterrorism. Turkey and Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, have moved towards closer economic and defence cooperation. Mecca institutionalizes these previously separate relationships within a trilateral framework that will include, according to the Turkish foreign minister, a ministerial committee and a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia. That detail is important as declarations of solidarity can be vague and fade over time. While institutions build continuity, create bureaucratic interests and shape expectations of their own. The three countries also bring complementary assets. Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, energy weight and a growing defence capability. Pakistan brings a large military, nuclear capability and decades of security cooperation with the Gulf states. Turkey contributes the most developed defence-industrial base of the three, a powerful conventional military, NATO membership and strategic geography. The combination does not amount to an alternative to NATO. Instead, it allows Ankara an opportunity to become the organizing power of a security network that exists outside the NATO alliance. Religion provides the narrative. Security provides the substance. The religious dimension of the agreement should be neither exaggerated nor ignored. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia share a common Islamic political vocabulary, and the choice of Mecca as the venue carries real symbolic weight. Their cooperation also reflects interests in deterrence, defence cooperation, military technology, regional stability and reducing dependence on external security providers. Religion supplies political legitimacy while security interests supply the substance. Yet, treating the agreement simply as religious solidarity risks underestimating the institutional components. Thus, its durability will depend on whether these interests remain aligned when a real crisis arrives. The Mecca agreement’s significance will ultimately be tested by a crisis. Suppose Saudi Arabia or Pakistan invokes the collective defence mechanism. Would Turkey respond according to its own national assessment, or consult NATO allies first? What happens if Washington and Ankara read the same crisis differently? These questions grow more consequential as the framework becomes institutionalized. Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, has stressed that the agreement is not directed against Iran or any other country, and that the form of assistance would be worked out through consultations after an attack. This makes the arrangement less rigid than Article 5 in practice. Flexibility does not eliminate strategic consequences. Ambiguous commitments leave room for manoeuvre while also leaving uncertainty about how partners will act once their interests diverge. For NATO this is a question of alliance cohesion. The Alliance has spent decades building integrated command structures, common standards and procedures for collective decision-making. The Mecca framework has none of this yet, so its political commitment currently runs well ahead of its demonstrated military capacity. That gap may narrow. This emerging duality for Turkey deserves particular attention in Europe. It sits at the intersection of Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia. It remains one of NATO’s most important military powers and is central to the Alliance’s southeastern flank. At the same time, Turkey has developed a foreign-policy network extending well beyond the Euro-Atlantic space. Its defence industry has become a central instrument of that strategy. Turkish drones, naval systems, armoured vehicles and missiles have created durable relationships with countries that share different formal alliances, alongside political and security ties across the Middle East, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Western Balkans. The Western Balkans are particularly relevant. Turkey has built its deepest security ties in the region with Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo – formalised in 2024 through comprehensive military framework agreements and reinforced by Turkey’s naval presence in Albania – while its cooperation with Bosnia and Herzegovina, though real, remains comparatively limited to bilateral training plans and equipment sales. Its growing defence-industrial presence gives these relationships an additional dimension. The Mecca agreement, however, goes one step further by building institutionalised collective security alongside bilateral and issue-specific ties Turkey has developed over the past decade. This is important for Europe as Turkish influence already shapes European security beyond NATO’s formal structures. The Black Sea is one such example. The Western Balkans are another. Turkey’s regional role is therefore becoming harder to read through the old question of whether Ankara is “turning towards” or “away from” the West. Turkey’s policies increasingly operate across several security environments at the same time. From strategic autonomy to strategic architecture The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. The S-400 purchase was one expression of this approach. The Mecca agreement suggests something further. Turkey is acquiring the ability to organise other states around its own security relationships. That is the difference between strategic autonomy and strategic architecture. An autonomous state seeks room to manoeuvre. A state capable of building its own security architecture can create room to manoeuvre for others as well. This gives Ankara an additional strategic asset and potentially greater leverage inside NATO. Turkey does not need an alternative to the Alliance to benefit from a parallel network. NATO membership raises the value of the new architecture because Ankara can draw on the Alliance’s credibility and capabilities while leading a separate structure outside it. That is the key to Turkish strategic duality. The Mecca agreement also fits in a broader shift in international security, in which regional powers increasingly hedge across overlapping partnerships rather than rely on one framework. Saudi Arabia maintains its relationship with the United States while deepening ties with Pakistan and Turkey. Pakistan combines its relationship with China with Gulf partnerships. Turkey stays in NATO while building its own networks. India has little reason to answer the Turkish-Pakistani relationship with a formal counter-bloc. Its likelier response is to deepen existing ties with Israel and the UAE. The pattern points towards a more fluid system of overlapping security networks in which states seek redundancy. A state can remain embedded in one security system while building another. The question is how these systems interact when their commitments collide. NATO has little reason to stop Turkey from developing legitimate partnerships outside the Alliance. Stronger regional capabilities can contribute to burden-sharing. The problem begins if an external framework creates obligations that conflict with Alliance priorities. The Mecca agreement has not reached that point yet. And there is no evidence of integrated command, common forces, joint operational planning or automatic intervention. Its mechanisms remain limited and its members retain wide freedom of interpretation. NATO should nevertheless follow how the framework develops. Its consultation mechanisms, intelligence cooperation, interoperability and defence-industrial cooperation will be important indicators of whether the agreement develops into a more substantial security structure. Turkey presents a particular case for the Alliance: a member developing a security network beyond NATO while remaining deeply embedded in the Alliance itself. That does not make Turkey an adversary; just a more complicated ally. It would be incorrect to say that the Mecca agreement establishes an “Islamic NATO”. What it does reveal, however, is Turkey’s ability to operate inside and outside established security structures simultaneously. The agreement may still fail to become a durable collective-defence mechanism. Members may disagree over priorities, new participants may decline to join, and its procedures may remain deliberately vague. Therefore, what matters is that Ankara is acquiring an institutional platform to organize security relationships beyond the Alliance while remaining one of its most strategically important members. For Europe, the lesson is that the old assumption that a country must choose between western alignment and strategic independence is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Turkey may be able to pursue both. The S-400 dispute forced Washington to confront the limits of Turkish autonomy in the military-technical sphere. The Mecca agreement may eventually force NATO and its European members to confront those same limits in the political-security sphere. Nevertheless, Turkey is not leaving NATO. Thus, the harder question is whether NATO is prepared for a Turkey that increasingly has something of its own to lead outside it. Nikola Lunić is a Serbian geopolitical and security analyst and Navy Captain (Ret.). He previously served as Serbia’s Defence Attaché in London and Oslo and as Executive Director of the Council for Strategic Policy. He currently works as a Strategic Affairs Consultant and is a regular guest lecturer at the Faculty of Law, University of Osijek.

At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms.
During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank.
However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century.
This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy.
Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency.
The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era.
Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers.

Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice.

Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible.

By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way.

extraction.body: The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. A new agreement with Middle East powers demonstrates just how Turkey is acquiring the ability to organize other states around its own security relationships. September 21, 2026 - Nikola Lunić - Articles and Commentary Turkey is not leaving NATO. The harder question is whether the Alliance can accommodate a member that is simultaneously building a security architecture of its own. The defence agreement signed in Mecca on August 7th by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan initially looked like another regional arrangement produced by a Middle East in turmoil. Its implications may extend well beyond the three signatories. The agreement declares that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described the mechanism as technically similar to NATO’s Article 5, while stressing that it is not directed against Iran or any other country. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has indicated that the framework could expand, with Egypt among the possible future participants. The significance of the agreement lies in what it reveals about Turkey’s evolving approach to power. Ankara has spent years pursuing greater strategic autonomy while remaining a member of the western alliance system. The Mecca agreement suggests that Ankara may now be moving towards something more ambitious: strategic duality, in which Turkey stays inside NATO while building security relationships outside it in which it can act as a leading power. That possibility deserves closer attention in Europe. Turkey’s acquisition of the Russian S-400 air defence system offers an instructive precedent. The dispute which erupted between Ankara and Washington was connected to a weapons purchase that the US judged incompatible with NATO’s security architecture and risky for the F-35 programme. Turkey was removed from the F-35 programme and faced sanctions in retaliation. The episode demonstrated that NATO membership does not give Ankara unlimited freedom to build capabilities that conflict with core Allied interests. The Mecca agreement, however, raises a different kind of issue. The S-400 could be kept outside a procurement programme, with its deployment restricted and its interoperability denied. A security commitment is harder to unwind. Once institutionalized through ministerial consultations, military planning, intelligence cooperation and expectations of mutual support, such a commitment acquires political momentum on its own. The Mecca framework, though still deliberately flexible, is already moving in that direction. The question for NATO concerns the point at which external partnerships develop into a second collective-security framework. That distinction may not matter today. It could matter enormously in a future crisis. The Mecca agreement did not create a security network from nothing. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already concluded a strategic mutual-defence agreement in September 2025, under which aggression against one would be regarded as aggression against both. Turkey and Pakistan have spent years deepening a defence relationship covering industry, technology and counterterrorism. Turkey and Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, have moved towards closer economic and defence cooperation. Mecca institutionalizes these previously separate relationships within a trilateral framework that will include, according to the Turkish foreign minister, a ministerial committee and a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia. That detail is important as declarations of solidarity can be vague and fade over time. While institutions build continuity, create bureaucratic interests and shape expectations of their own. The three countries also bring complementary assets. Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, energy weight and a growing defence capability. Pakistan brings a large military, nuclear capability and decades of security cooperation with the Gulf states. Turkey contributes the most developed defence-industrial base of the three, a powerful conventional military, NATO membership and strategic geography. The combination does not amount to an alternative to NATO. Instead, it allows Ankara an opportunity to become the organizing power of a security network that exists outside the NATO alliance. Religion provides the narrative. Security provides the substance. The religious dimension of the agreement should be neither exaggerated nor ignored. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia share a common Islamic political vocabulary, and the choice of Mecca as the venue carries real symbolic weight. Their cooperation also reflects interests in deterrence, defence cooperation, military technology, regional stability and reducing dependence on external security providers. Religion supplies political legitimacy while security interests supply the substance. Yet, treating the agreement simply as religious solidarity risks underestimating the institutional components. Thus, its durability will depend on whether these interests remain aligned when a real crisis arrives. The Mecca agreement’s significance will ultimately be tested by a crisis. Suppose Saudi Arabia or Pakistan invokes the collective defence mechanism. Would Turkey respond according to its own national assessment, or consult NATO allies first? What happens if Washington and Ankara read the same crisis differently? These questions grow more consequential as the framework becomes institutionalized. Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, has stressed that the agreement is not directed against Iran or any other country, and that the form of assistance would be worked out through consultations after an attack. This makes the arrangement less rigid than Article 5 in practice. Flexibility does not eliminate strategic consequences. Ambiguous commitments leave room for manoeuvre while also leaving uncertainty about how partners will act once their interests diverge. For NATO this is a question of alliance cohesion. The Alliance has spent decades building integrated command structures, common standards and procedures for collective decision-making. The Mecca framework has none of this yet, so its political commitment currently runs well ahead of its demonstrated military capacity. That gap may narrow. This emerging duality for Turkey deserves particular attention in Europe. It sits at the intersection of Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia. It remains one of NATO’s most important military powers and is central to the Alliance’s southeastern flank. At the same time, Turkey has developed a foreign-policy network extending well beyond the Euro-Atlantic space. Its defence industry has become a central instrument of that strategy. Turkish drones, naval systems, armoured vehicles and missiles have created durable relationships with countries that share different formal alliances, alongside political and security ties across the Middle East, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Western Balkans. The Western Balkans are particularly relevant. Turkey has built its deepest security ties in the region with Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo – formalised in 2024 through comprehensive military framework agreements and reinforced by Turkey’s naval presence in Albania – while its cooperation with Bosnia and Herzegovina, though real, remains comparatively limited to bilateral training plans and equipment sales. Its growing defence-industrial presence gives these relationships an additional dimension. The Mecca agreement, however, goes one step further by building institutionalised collective security alongside bilateral and issue-specific ties Turkey has developed over the past decade. This is important for Europe as Turkish influence already shapes European security beyond NATO’s formal structures. The Black Sea is one such example. The Western Balkans are another. Turkey’s regional role is therefore becoming harder to read through the old question of whether Ankara is “turning towards” or “away from” the West. Turkey’s policies increasingly operate across several security environments at the same time. From strategic autonomy to strategic architecture The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. The S-400 purchase was one expression of this approach. The Mecca agreement suggests something further. Turkey is acquiring the ability to organise other states around its own security relationships. That is the difference between strategic autonomy and strategic architecture. An autonomous state seeks room to manoeuvre. A state capable of building its own security architecture can create room to manoeuvre for others as well. This gives Ankara an additional strategic asset and potentially greater leverage inside NATO. Turkey does not need an alternative to the Alliance to benefit from a parallel network. NATO membership raises the value of the new architecture because Ankara can draw on the Alliance’s credibility and capabilities while leading a separate structure outside it. That is the key to Turkish strategic duality. The Mecca agreement also fits in a broader shift in international security, in which regional powers increasingly hedge across overlapping partnerships rather than rely on one framework. Saudi Arabia maintains its relationship with the United States while deepening ties with Pakistan and Turkey. Pakistan combines its relationship with China with Gulf partnerships. Turkey stays in NATO while building its own networks. India has little reason to answer the Turkish-Pakistani relationship with a formal counter-bloc. Its likelier response is to deepen existing ties with Israel and the UAE. The pattern points towards a more fluid system of overlapping security networks in which states seek redundancy. A state can remain embedded in one security system while building another. The question is how these systems interact when their commitments collide. NATO has little reason to stop Turkey from developing legitimate partnerships outside the Alliance. Stronger regional capabilities can contribute to burden-sharing. The problem begins if an external framework creates obligations that conflict with Alliance priorities. The Mecca agreement has not reached that point yet. And there is no evidence of integrated command, common forces, joint operational planning or automatic intervention. Its mechanisms remain limited and its members retain wide freedom of interpretation. NATO should nevertheless follow how the framework develops. Its consultation mechanisms, intelligence cooperation, interoperability and defence-industrial cooperation will be important indicators of whether the agreement develops into a more substantial security structure. Turkey presents a particular case for the Alliance: a member developing a security network beyond NATO while remaining deeply embedded in the Alliance itself. That does not make Turkey an adversary; just a more complicated ally. It would be incorrect to say that the Mecca agreement establishes an “Islamic NATO”. What it does reveal, however, is Turkey’s ability to operate inside and outside established security structures simultaneously. The agreement may still fail to become a durable collective-defence mechanism. Members may disagree over priorities, new participants may decline to join, and its procedures may remain deliberately vague. Therefore, what matters is that Ankara is acquiring an institutional platform to organize security relationships beyond the Alliance while remaining one of its most strategically important members. For Europe, the lesson is that the old assumption that a country must choose between western alignment and strategic independence is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Turkey may be able to pursue both. The S-400 dispute forced Washington to confront the limits of Turkish autonomy in the military-technical sphere. The Mecca agreement may eventually force NATO and its European members to confront those same limits in the political-security sphere. Nevertheless, Turkey is not leaving NATO. Thus, the harder question is whether NATO is prepared for a Turkey that increasingly has something of its own to lead outside it. Nikola Lunić is a Serbian geopolitical and security analyst and Navy Captain (Ret.). passages: The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. A new agreement with Middle East powers demonstrates just how Turkey is acquiring the ability to organize other states around its own security relationships.
September 21, 2026 - Nikola Lunić - Articles and Commentary

Turkey is not leaving NATO. The harder question is whether the Alliance can accommodate a member that is simultaneously building a security architecture of its own. The defence agreement signed in Mecca on August 7th by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan initially looked like another regional arrangement produced by a Middle East in turmoil. Its implications may extend well beyond the three signatories.

The agreement declares that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described the mechanism as technically similar to NATO’s Article 5, while stressing that it is not directed against Iran or any other country. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has indicated that the framework could expand, with Egypt among the possible future participants.

The significance of the agreement lies in what it reveals about Turkey’s evolving approach to power. Ankara has spent years pursuing greater strategic autonomy while remaining a member of the western alliance system. The Mecca agreement suggests that Ankara may now be moving towards something more ambitious: strategic duality, in which Turkey stays inside NATO while building security relationships outside it in which it can act as a leading power. That possibility deserves closer attention in Europe.

Turkey’s acquisition of the Russian S-400 air defence system offers an instructive precedent. The dispute which erupted between Ankara and Washington was connected to a weapons purchase that the US judged incompatible with NATO’s security architecture and risky for the F-35 programme. Turkey was removed from the F-35 programme and faced sanctions in retaliation. The episode demonstrated that NATO membership does not give Ankara unlimited freedom to build capabilities that conflict with core Allied interests.

The Mecca agreement, however, raises a different kind of issue. The S-400 could be kept outside a procurement programme, with its deployment restricted and its interoperability denied. A security commitment is harder to unwind. Once institutionalized through ministerial consultations, military planning, intelligence cooperation and expectations of mutual support, such a commitment acquires political momentum on its own. The Mecca framework, though still deliberately flexible, is already moving in that direction. The question for NATO concerns the point at which external partnerships develop into a second collective-security framework. That distinction may not matter today. It could matter enormously in a future crisis.

The Mecca agreement did not create a security network from nothing. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already concluded a strategic mutual-defence agreement in September 2025, under which aggression against one would be regarded as aggression against both. Turkey and Pakistan have spent years deepening a defence relationship covering industry, technology and counterterrorism. Turkey and Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, have moved towards closer economic and defence cooperation. Mecca institutionalizes these previously separate relationships within a trilateral framework that will include, according to the Turkish foreign minister, a ministerial committee and a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia.

That detail is important as declarations of solidarity can be vague and fade over time. While institutions build continuity, create bureaucratic interests and shape expectations of their own. The three countries also bring complementary assets. Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, energy weight and a growing defence capability. Pakistan brings a large military, nuclear capability and decades of security cooperation with the Gulf states. Turkey contributes the most developed defence-industrial base of the three, a powerful conventional military, NATO membership and strategic geography.
The combination does not amount to an alternative to NATO. Instead, it allows Ankara an opportunity to become the organizing power of a security network that exists outside the NATO alliance.
Religion provides the narrative. Security provides the substance.

The religious dimension of the agreement should be neither exaggerated nor ignored. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia share a common Islamic political vocabulary, and the choice of Mecca as the venue carries real symbolic weight. Their cooperation also reflects interests in deterrence, defence cooperation, military technology, regional stability and reducing dependence on external security providers. Religion supplies political legitimacy while security interests supply the substance. Yet, treating the agreement simply as religious solidarity risks underestimating the institutional components. Thus, its durability will depend on whether these interests remain aligned when a real crisis arrives.

The Mecca agreement’s significance will ultimately be tested by a crisis. Suppose Saudi Arabia or Pakistan invokes the collective defence mechanism. Would Turkey respond according to its own national assessment, or consult NATO allies first? What happens if Washington and Ankara read the same crisis differently? These questions grow more consequential as the framework becomes institutionalized.

Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, has stressed that the agreement is not directed against Iran or any other country, and that the form of assistance would be worked out through consultations after an attack. This makes the arrangement less rigid than Article 5 in practice. Flexibility does not eliminate strategic consequences. Ambiguous commitments leave room for manoeuvre while also leaving uncertainty about how partners will act once their interests diverge. For NATO this is a question of alliance cohesion.

The Alliance has spent decades building integrated command structures, common standards and procedures for collective decision-making. The Mecca framework has none of this yet, so its political commitment currently runs well ahead of its demonstrated military capacity. That gap may narrow.

This emerging duality for Turkey deserves particular attention in Europe. It sits at the intersection of Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia. It remains one of NATO’s most important military powers and is central to the Alliance’s southeastern flank. At the same time, Turkey has developed a foreign-policy network extending well beyond the Euro-Atlantic space. Its defence industry has become a central instrument of that strategy. Turkish drones, naval systems, armoured vehicles and missiles have created durable relationships with countries that share different formal alliances, alongside political and security ties across the Middle East, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Western Balkans.

The Western Balkans are particularly relevant. Turkey has built its deepest security ties in the region with Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo – formalised in 2024 through comprehensive military framework agreements and reinforced by Turkey’s naval presence in Albania – while its cooperation with Bosnia and Herzegovina, though real, remains comparatively limited to bilateral training plans and equipment sales. Its growing defence-industrial presence gives these relationships an additional dimension.

The Mecca agreement, however, goes one step further by building institutionalised collective security alongside bilateral and issue-specific ties Turkey has developed over the past decade. This is important for Europe as Turkish influence already shapes European security beyond NATO’s formal structures. The Black Sea is one such example. The Western Balkans are another. Turkey’s regional role is therefore becoming harder to read through the old question of whether Ankara is “turning towards” or “away from” the West. Turkey’s policies increasingly operate across several security environments at the same time.
From strategic autonomy to strategic architecture

The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. The S-400 purchase was one expression of this approach. The Mecca agreement suggests something further. Turkey is acquiring the ability to organise other states around its own security relationships. That is the difference between strategic autonomy and strategic architecture. An autonomous state seeks room to manoeuvre. A state capable of building its own security architecture can create room to manoeuvre for others as well. This gives Ankara an additional strategic asset and potentially greater leverage inside NATO.

Turkey does not need an alternative to the Alliance to benefit from a parallel network. NATO membership raises the value of the new architecture because Ankara can draw on the Alliance’s credibility and capabilities while leading a separate structure outside it. That is the key to Turkish strategic duality.

The Mecca agreement also fits in a broader shift in international security, in which regional powers increasingly hedge across overlapping partnerships rather than rely on one framework. Saudi Arabia maintains its relationship with the United States while deepening ties with Pakistan and Turkey. Pakistan combines its relationship with China with Gulf partnerships. Turkey stays in NATO while building its own networks. India has little reason to answer the Turkish-Pakistani relationship with a formal counter-bloc. Its likelier response is to deepen existing ties with Israel and the UAE.

The pattern points towards a more fluid system of overlapping security networks in which states seek redundancy. A state can remain embedded in one security system while building another. The question is how these systems interact when their commitments collide.

NATO has little reason to stop Turkey from developing legitimate partnerships outside the Alliance. Stronger regional capabilities can contribute to burden-sharing. The problem begins if an external framework creates obligations that conflict with Alliance priorities. The Mecca agreement has not reached that point yet. And there is no evidence of integrated command, common forces, joint operational planning or automatic intervention. Its mechanisms remain limited and its members retain wide freedom of interpretation. NATO should nevertheless follow how the framework develops. Its consultation mechanisms, intelligence cooperation, interoperability and defence-industrial cooperation will be important indicators of whether the agreement develops into a more substantial security structure.

Turkey presents a particular case for the Alliance: a member developing a security network beyond NATO while remaining deeply embedded in the Alliance itself. That does not make Turkey an adversary; just a more complicated ally.

It would be incorrect to say that the Mecca agreement establishes an “Islamic NATO”. What it does reveal, however, is Turkey’s ability to operate inside and outside established security structures simultaneously. The agreement may still fail to become a durable collective-defence mechanism. Members may disagree over priorities, new participants may decline to join, and its procedures may remain deliberately vague. Therefore, what matters is that Ankara is acquiring an institutional platform to organize security relationships beyond the Alliance while remaining one of its most strategically important members.

For Europe, the lesson is that the old assumption that a country must choose between western alignment and strategic independence is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Turkey may be able to pursue both. The S-400 dispute forced Washington to confront the limits of Turkish autonomy in the military-technical sphere. The Mecca agreement may eventually force NATO and its European members to confront those same limits in the political-security sphere.
Nevertheless, Turkey is not leaving NATO. Thus, the harder question is whether NATO is prepared for a Turkey that increasingly has something of its own to lead outside it.

Nikola Lunić is a Serbian geopolitical and security analyst and Navy Captain (Ret.). He previously served as Serbia’s Defence Attaché in London and Oslo and as Executive Director of the Council for Strategic Policy. He currently works as a Strategic Affairs Consultant and is a regular guest lecturer at the Faculty of Law, University of Osijek.

passages: The LA Sparks announced plans to honor Hall of Fame center Lisa Leslie with a statue outside Crypto.com Arena.
She becomes just the second player in WNBA history to receive such recognition from a former franchise.
Lisa Leslie spent her entire 12-year career with the Sparks after joining the league at its 1997 inception.
The eight-time All-Star led LA to back-to-back championships in 2001 and 2002, earning three MVP awards and four Olympic gold medals during her playing career.
Lisa Leslie says Kobe Bryant ‘was really like a little brother’
"To be cemented in Los Angeles, the city that raised me, I couldn't be more proud," Leslie said in a team statement .
Lisa Leslie Calls Marina Mabrey a "Game-Changer" in the Latest 'Fast Friends'
Leslie holds the Sparks' all-time records in points, rebounds, blocks, field goals, free throws, minutes, and games.
Her eight First Team All-WNBA selections rank second all-time.
Lisa Leslie Talks Post-WNBA Success on '1v1 with Kelley O'Hara'
Sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany are behind the piece.
The ceremony takes place September 20th, before the Sparks host 2026 WNBA expansion side Portland.

Lisa Leslie spent her entire 12-year career with the Sparks after joining the league at its 1997 inception.
The eight-time All-Star led LA to back-to-back championships in 2001 and 2002, earning three MVP awards and four Olympic gold medals during her playing career.
Lisa Leslie says Kobe Bryant ‘was really like a little brother’
"To be cemented in Los Angeles, the city that raised me, I couldn't be more proud," Leslie said in a team statement .
Lisa Leslie Calls Marina Mabrey a "Game-Changer" in the Latest 'Fast Friends'
Leslie holds the Sparks' all-time records in points, rebounds, blocks, field goals, free throws, minutes, and games.
Her eight First Team All-WNBA selections rank second all-time.
Lisa Leslie Talks Post-WNBA Success on '1v1 with Kelley O'Hara'
Sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany are behind the piece.
The ceremony takes place September 20th, before the Sparks host 2026 WNBA expansion side Portland.

A statue honoring Naismith Basketball Hall of Famer Lisa Leslie was unveiled Sunday outside Crypto.com Arena, where she played the final eight seasons of her 12-season WNBA career, all with the Los Angeles Sparks.

Leslie thanked fans for their support and recalled her interactions with them during a halftime speech at the Sparks' 105-84 victory over the Portland Fire on Sunday.
Leslie played for the Sparks from their inaugural season in 1997 through 2009, missing the 2007 season because she was pregnant.
The statue, created by sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany, depicts Leslie dunking an orange-and-white WNBA basketball, a feat she accomplished in 2002.

extraction.body: The LA Sparks announced plans to honor Hall of Fame center Lisa Leslie with a statue outside Crypto.com Arena. She becomes just the second player in WNBA history to receive such recognition from a former franchise. "To be cemented in Los Angeles, the city that raised me, I couldn't be more proud," Leslie said in a team statement . "God has blessed me and I have truly given my all to this sport and our community." Lisa Leslie spent her entire 12-year career with the Sparks after joining the league at its 1997 inception. The eight-time All-Star led LA to back-to-back championships in 2001 and 2002, earning three MVP awards and four Olympic gold medals during her playing career. Leslie holds the Sparks' all-time records in points, rebounds, blocks, field goals, free throws, minutes, and games. She ranks third in WNBA history in double-doubles and blocks, while sitting sixth in rebounds, ninth in offensive rebounds, and 13th in scoring. Her eight First Team All-WNBA selections rank second all-time. Leslie made history as the first player to dunk during a WNBA game. The move single-handedly helped redefine women's basketball on its biggest stage. After retiring in 2009, Leslie built a successful broadcasting and media career. The Sparks retired her No. 9 jersey in 2010. Leslie joins 15 other sports legends honored outside Crypto.com Arena, including Lakers greats Magic Johnson, Kobe Bryant, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Shaquille O'Neal . "Lisa's legacy isn't just measured by championships and accolades," said Johnson. "She is a pioneer, a cultural icon, and a force who elevated women's basketball to new heights." Sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany are behind the piece. The ceremony takes place September 20th, before the Sparks host 2026 WNBA expansion side Portland. The statue, created by sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany, depicts Leslie dunking an orange-and-white WNBA basketball, a feat she accomplished in 2002. She was the first player in league history to dunk in a game, five years after missing a dunk attempt in the WNBA's inaugural game.

I left it out here on the floor because that's what you deserve as fans.”

Leslie said she viewed every game as “a moment to change the mind of a man who was a hater. It was a chance to convince somebody who didn't believe in women's basketball. Bitcoin critic Peter Schiff said Friday’s Bitcoin price increase following the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s tokenized stock announcement was illogical and bearish for the cryptocurrency .
In an X post on Saturday, Schiff argued that tokenized securities backed by profitable companies offer a superior store of value compared with Bitcoin (BTC) .

Yesterday’s big Bitcoin rally following the SEC’s tokenized stock announcement makes no sense. The news is actually bearish for Bitcoin, which must now compete with tokenized securities. Digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a superior,…

Schiff described the Bitcoin rally as disconnected from the substance of the SEC announcement. He said digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a more reliable store of value than a token backed by nothing.
Tokenized stocks, in his view, provide the conveniences associated with Bitcoin without the risk he associated with a decentralized structure that could collapse.

On September 17, the SEC announced a five-year conditional innovation exemption for qualifying blockchain-based trading venues. The order allows Tokenized Securities Venues to facilitate trading in certain National Market System stocks under specified conditions.

It provides relief from certain Exchange Act exchange and dealer requirements and permits the use of permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools. The exemption is temporary and conditional rather than a permanent regulatory framework.

Bitcoin witnessed a notable surge after the announcement and crossed the $80,000 mark on Friday . At the time of this writing (on September 19 at 2:00 pm UTC), the asset traded at $81,290.43 on Saturday, September 19, 2026, according to CoinGecko data, up 1.6 percent over the prior 24 hours.

Bitcoin’s 24-hour range was $79,925.66 to $81,674.72. Its seven-day range was $75,038.12 to $81,674.72. Bitcoin’s all-time high of $126,080 was recorded on October 6, 2025.

For third-party wrappers, the order requires distribution or availability of related proxy materials and other issuer communications at no cost to the issuer or shareholders. Dividends, voting rights and proxy distribution are required under the text of the order, Thorn said.

Bitcoin critic Peter Schiff said Friday’s Bitcoin price increase following the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s tokenized stock announcement was illogical and bearish for the cryptocurrency . In an X post on Saturday, Schiff argued that tokenized securities backed by profitable companies offer a superior store of value compared with Bitcoin (BTC) . Yesterday’s big Bitcoin rally following the SEC’s tokenized stock announcement makes no sense. The news is actually bearish for Bitcoin, which must now compete with tokenized securities. Digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a superior,… Schiff described the Bitcoin rally as disconnected from the substance of the SEC announcement. He said digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a more reliable store of value than a token backed by nothing. Tokenized stocks, in his view, provide the conveniences associated with Bitcoin without the risk he associated with a decentralized structure that could collapse. On September 17, the SEC announced a five-year conditional innovation exemption for qualifying blockchain-based trading venues. The order allows Tokenized Securities Venues to facilitate trading in certain National Market System stocks under specified conditions. It provides relief from certain Exchange Act exchange and dealer requirements and permits the use of permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools. The exemption is temporary and conditional rather than a permanent regulatory framework. Bitcoin witnessed a notable surge after the announcement and crossed the $80,000 mark on Friday . At the time of this writing (on September 19 at 2:00 pm UTC), the asset traded at $81,290.43 on Saturday, September 19, 2026, according to CoinGecko data, up 1.6 percent over the prior 24 hours. Bitcoin’s 24-hour range was $79,925.66 to $81,674.72. Its seven-day range was $75,038.12 to $81,674.72. Market capitalization was listed at $1.633 trillion, with 24-hour trading volume of $35.698 billion. Circulating supply totaled 20.087 million BTC against a maximum supply of 21 million. Bitcoin’s all-time high of $126,080 was recorded on October 6, 2025. Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, stated that the order includes specific requirements . According to Thorn , a tokenized venue must verify that the token provides holders the same rights and privileges as traditional NMS stock of an equivalent class. For third-party wrappers, the order requires distribution or availability of related proxy materials and other issuer communications at no cost to the issuer or shareholders. Dividends, voting rights and proxy distribution are required under the text of the order, Thorn said. Comments posted on the platform X addressed Schiff’s remarks, rejecting his theory. The 20 Delta Guy said Bitcoin could move substantially higher and that Schiff has issued repeated warnings of declines that have not occurred, adding that he should move on. Rabbi Nakamoto stated that Schiff is emotionally opposed to Bitcoin and that no amount of logical explanation would alter that position , wishing him a nice weekend. The mechanism here is that the issuers of Bitcoin ETFs need to buy coins to back their ETF shares. U.S.-based ETFs absorbed about $3.8 billion in net inflows over the three weeks through Sept. 4, per SoSoValue data, including $730.8 million in inflows on Sept. 3 alone.
