passages: The NATO Summit to be held in Ankara in 2026 represents a critical meeting that will reopen the debate on Turkey’s position within the Alliance.
This summit should not be regarded merely as one of NATO’s routine diplomatic meetings that sets the Alliance’s agenda.

Indeed, this historical context demonstrates that Turkey is emerging not only as the host country, but also as a central actor capable of reading the eastern and southern axes of the European security order simultaneously.

While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns.
The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question.
Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges.

At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms.
During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank.
However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century.
This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy.
Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency.
The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era.
Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers.

Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice.
In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas.

From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale.
Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible.

By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way.

extraction.body: The NATO Summit to be held in Ankara in 2026 represents a critical meeting that will reopen the debate on Turkey’s position within the Alliance. This summit should not be regarded merely as one of NATO’s routine diplomatic meetings that sets the Alliance’s agenda. It will also serve as a platform through which Turkey’s place in the Western security architecture, its strategic weight within the Alliance, and its multidimensional foreign policy capacity will become more visible amid the fragile security perceptions currently shaping the West. For this reason, the summit to be held in Ankara on 7–8 July 2026 will, in a sense, also constitute a moment of self-questioning for the Western security alliance. Indeed, this historical context demonstrates that Turkey is emerging not only as the host country, but also as a central actor capable of reading the eastern and southern axes of the European security order simultaneously. The most significant meaning of the Ankara Summit for Turkey lies in the fact that Turkey’s position within NATO can no longer be explained solely through geographical advantage, military capacity, or historical membership. During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank. However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century. Turkey is no longer merely a security buffer located on the margins of the Alliance; rather, it has become a constitutive security actor situated at the intersection of the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Balkans, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and critical energy transit routes. In this respect, the Ankara Summit provides an important platform for discussing Turkey’s evolving position beyond its traditional role within NATO. Turkey’s position within NATO has increasingly been redefined through its defense industry capacity. The country is no longer merely a state that uses NATO weapons systems or contributes to the Alliance’s military planning because of its geographical location. Through its growing capabilities in unmanned aerial vehicles, land systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, air defense systems and ammunition production, Turkey has become an actor that strengthens its own defense production infrastructure within the Alliance and transforms this capacity into an instrument of foreign policy. This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy. Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency. Instead, it does so by developing its national capabilities, becoming a producing actor in the defense industry, therefore prioritizing its own security concerns when necessary. This gives Turkey a new bargaining space within NATO and moves Ankara’s position in the Alliance onto a more autonomous, flexible and multidimensional ground. Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges. European countries need Turkey’s military capacity, geographical position, role in migration management, and influence over the Black Sea, Caucasus, etc. At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms. This contradiction constitutes one of the most important structural problems behind the Ankara NATO Summit. Turkey is indispensable for European security, yet its institutional place within the European security architecture remains contested and insufficiently defined. For this reason, the Ankara Summit will not merely mean that Turkey is hosting NATO. It will also provide Turkey with an opportunity to present its own security agenda to the Alliance, to reveal the narrowing of Europe’s security understanding, and to underline the necessity of evaluating multidimensional crisis areas together. In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas. From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale. At this point, Turkey’s significance stems not only from its proximity to crisis regions, but also from its ability to read these crises simultaneously and to understand the connections between them. Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible. By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way. Therefore, the Ankara Summit is not only a security meeting; it is also a reflection of changing hegemonic relations in the global system, internal tensions within the Western alliance, and Turkey’s capacity to grasp this transformation. The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era. Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers. Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice. Ankara’s defense industry breakthrough, multidimensional diplomacy, direct engagement with crisis regions and more autonomous position within NATO show that Turkey is not passively observing changing global power balances. Rather, it is trying to open its own space within this transformation. The Ankara NATO Summit demonstrates that Turkey has moved beyond its traditional position within NATO and has become a strategic actor capable of managing the duality within the Western security architecture. While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns. In this regard, the fundamental question of the Ankara Summit is the following: will NATO and Europe continue to see Turkey merely as a military capacity and geographical advantage needed in times of crisis, or will they recognize Turkey as a constitutive, transformative and strategic actor in the reconstruction of the European security architecture? The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question. passages: The significance of the agreement lies in what it reveals about Turkey’s evolving approach to power.
Ankara has spent years pursuing greater strategic autonomy while remaining a member of the western alliance system.

The Mecca agreement suggests that Ankara may now be moving towards something more ambitious: strategic duality, in which Turkey stays inside NATO while building security relationships outside it in which it can act as a leading power.
That possibility deserves closer attention in Europe.
This is important for Europe as Turkish influence already shapes European security beyond NATO’s formal structures.
Turkey’s regional role is therefore becoming harder to read through the old question of whether Ankara is “turning towards” or “away from” the West.
Turkey’s policies increasingly operate across several security environments at the same time.
The dispute which erupted between Ankara and Washington was connected to a weapons purchase that the US judged incompatible with NATO’s security architecture and risky for the F-35 programme.
The episode demonstrated that NATO membership does not give Ankara unlimited freedom to build capabilities that conflict with core Allied interests.
The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power.
The S-400 purchase was one expression of this approach.
Turkey is acquiring the ability to organise other states around its own security relationships.
That is the difference between strategic autonomy and strategic architecture.
This gives Ankara an additional strategic asset and potentially greater leverage inside NATO.
The harder question is whether the Alliance can accommodate a member that is simultaneously building a security architecture of its own.
The defence agreement signed in Mecca on August 7th by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan initially looked like another regional arrangement produced by a Middle East in turmoil.
Its implications may extend well beyond the three signatories.
It sits at the intersection of Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia.
It remains one of NATO’s most important military powers and is central to the Alliance’s southeastern flank.
Its defence industry has become a central instrument of that strategy.
That does not make Turkey an adversary; just a more complicated ally.
For Europe, the lesson is that the old assumption that a country must choose between western alignment and strategic independence is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.
That detail is important as declarations of solidarity can be vague and fade over time.

coreStoryFacts.text: The NATO Summit to be held in Ankara in 2026 represents a critical meeting that will reopen the debate on Turkey’s position within the Alliance.
This summit should not be regarded merely as one of NATO’s routine diplomatic meetings that sets the Alliance’s agenda.

Indeed, this historical context demonstrates that Turkey is emerging not only as the host country, but also as a central actor capable of reading the eastern and southern axes of the European security order simultaneously.

While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns.
The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question.
Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges.

At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms.
During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank.
However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century.
This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy.
Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency.
The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era.
Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers.

Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice.
In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas.

From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale.
Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible.

By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way.

extraction.body: The NATO Summit to be held in Ankara in 2026 represents a critical meeting that will reopen the debate on Turkey’s position within the Alliance. This summit should not be regarded merely as one of NATO’s routine diplomatic meetings that sets the Alliance’s agenda. It will also serve as a platform through which Turkey’s place in the Western security architecture, its strategic weight within the Alliance, and its multidimensional foreign policy capacity will become more visible amid the fragile security perceptions currently shaping the West. For this reason, the summit to be held in Ankara on 7–8 July 2026 will, in a sense, also constitute a moment of self-questioning for the Western security alliance. Indeed, this historical context demonstrates that Turkey is emerging not only as the host country, but also as a central actor capable of reading the eastern and southern axes of the European security order simultaneously. The most significant meaning of the Ankara Summit for Turkey lies in the fact that Turkey’s position within NATO can no longer be explained solely through geographical advantage, military capacity, or historical membership. During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank. However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century. Turkey is no longer merely a security buffer located on the margins of the Alliance; rather, it has become a constitutive security actor situated at the intersection of the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Balkans, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and critical energy transit routes. In this respect, the Ankara Summit provides an important platform for discussing Turkey’s evolving position beyond its traditional role within NATO. Turkey’s position within NATO has increasingly been redefined through its defense industry capacity. The country is no longer merely a state that uses NATO weapons systems or contributes to the Alliance’s military planning because of its geographical location. Through its growing capabilities in unmanned aerial vehicles, land systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, air defense systems and ammunition production, Turkey has become an actor that strengthens its own defense production infrastructure within the Alliance and transforms this capacity into an instrument of foreign policy. This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy. Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency. Instead, it does so by developing its national capabilities, becoming a producing actor in the defense industry, therefore prioritizing its own security concerns when necessary. This gives Turkey a new bargaining space within NATO and moves Ankara’s position in the Alliance onto a more autonomous, flexible and multidimensional ground. Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges. European countries need Turkey’s military capacity, geographical position, role in migration management, and influence over the Black Sea, Caucasus, etc. At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms. This contradiction constitutes one of the most important structural problems behind the Ankara NATO Summit. Turkey is indispensable for European security, yet its institutional place within the European security architecture remains contested and insufficiently defined. For this reason, the Ankara Summit will not merely mean that Turkey is hosting NATO. It will also provide Turkey with an opportunity to present its own security agenda to the Alliance, to reveal the narrowing of Europe’s security understanding, and to underline the necessity of evaluating multidimensional crisis areas together. In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas. From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale. At this point, Turkey’s significance stems not only from its proximity to crisis regions, but also from its ability to read these crises simultaneously and to understand the connections between them. Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible. By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way. Therefore, the Ankara Summit is not only a security meeting; it is also a reflection of changing hegemonic relations in the global system, internal tensions within the Western alliance, and Turkey’s capacity to grasp this transformation. The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era. Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers. Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice. Ankara’s defense industry breakthrough, multidimensional diplomacy, direct engagement with crisis regions and more autonomous position within NATO show that Turkey is not passively observing changing global power balances. Rather, it is trying to open its own space within this transformation. The Ankara NATO Summit demonstrates that Turkey has moved beyond its traditional position within NATO and has become a strategic actor capable of managing the duality within the Western security architecture. While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns. In this regard, the fundamental question of the Ankara Summit is the following: will NATO and Europe continue to see Turkey merely as a military capacity and geographical advantage needed in times of crisis, or will they recognize Turkey as a constitutive, transformative and strategic actor in the reconstruction of the European security architecture? The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question. The most significant meaning of the Ankara Summit for Turkey lies in the fact that Turkey’s position within NATO can no longer be explained solely through geographical advantage, military capacity, or historical membership. During the Cold War, Turkey was largely perceived as NATO’s forward outpost on the southeastern flank. However, this role has transformed in the twenty-first century. Turkey is no longer merely a security buffer located on the margins of the Alliance; rather, it has become a constitutive security actor situated at the intersection of the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Balkans, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and critical energy transit routes. In this respect, the Ankara Summit provides an important platform for discussing Turkey’s evolving position beyond its traditional role within NATO.

Turkey’s position within NATO has increasingly been redefined through its defense industry capacity. The country is no longer merely a state that uses NATO weapons systems or contributes to the Alliance’s military planning because of its geographical location. Through its growing capabilities in unmanned aerial vehicles, land systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, air defense systems and ammunition production, Turkey has become an actor that strengthens its own defense production infrastructure within the Alliance and transforms this capacity into an instrument of foreign policy.

This development increases Turkey’s strategic value within NATO while also strengthening Ankara’s search for strategic autonomy. Turkey contributes to NATO; however, it does not provide this contribution solely within a relationship of dependency. Instead, it does so by developing its national capabilities, becoming a producing actor in the defense industry, therefore prioritizing its own security concerns when necessary. This gives Turkey a new bargaining space within NATO and moves Ankara’s position in the Alliance onto a more autonomous, flexible and multidimensional ground.

Yet it is precisely at this point that the duality within the Western security architecture emerges. European countries need Turkey’s military capacity, geographical position, role in migration management, and influence over the Black Sea, Caucasus, etc. At the same time, however, Europe often places Turkey in an exclusionary, restrictive or secondary position with regard to defense industry cooperation, the EU accession process, Eastern Mediterranean policy, human rights discourse and strategic decision-making mechanisms. This contradiction constitutes one of the most important structural problems behind the Ankara NATO Summit. Turkey is indispensable for European security, yet its institutional place within the European security architecture remains contested and insufficiently defined.

For this reason, the Ankara Summit will not merely mean that Turkey is hosting NATO. It will also provide Turkey with an opportunity to present its own security agenda to the Alliance, to reveal the narrowing of Europe’s security understanding, and to underline the necessity of evaluating multidimensional crisis areas together. In today’s international system, wars and conflicts can no longer be interpreted only as security issues confined to specific geographical areas. From Ukraine to Gaza, from the Black Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean, from Iran-centered tensions to energy corridors, current crises demonstrate that security perceptions are increasingly interconnected on a global scale.

At this point, Turkey’s significance stems not only from its proximity to crisis regions, but also from its ability to read these crises simultaneously and to understand the connections between them. Interpreting wars merely as military security issues makes it more difficult to understand under what conditions peace may become possible. By contrast, analyzing wars through security perceptions, power balances, hegemonic struggles, energy dependencies, migration movements and regional fragilities makes it possible to discuss peace in a more realistic way. Therefore, the Ankara Summit is not only a security meeting; it is also a reflection of changing hegemonic relations in the global system, internal tensions within the Western alliance, and Turkey’s capacity to grasp this transformation.

The global system is moving away from the unipolar security understanding of the post-Cold War era. Power, technology, energy, defense production and diplomatic influence are being redistributed among different centers. Within this transformation, Turkey emerges not merely as an actor adapting to the existing security architecture, but as a country that captures the transformation of this architecture on the ground and translates it into its own foreign policy practice. Ankara’s defense industry breakthrough, multidimensional diplomacy, direct engagement with crisis regions and more autonomous position within NATO show that Turkey is not passively observing changing global power balances. Rather, it is trying to open its own space within this transformation.

The Ankara NATO Summit demonstrates that Turkey has moved beyond its traditional position within NATO and has become a strategic actor capable of managing the duality within the Western security architecture. While Turkey continues to fulfil its alliance responsibilities, it also brings its own security agenda to NATO through issues such as the defense industry, energy security, migration management and regional concerns. In this regard, the fundamental question of the Ankara Summit is the following: will NATO and Europe continue to see Turkey merely as a military capacity and geographical advantage needed in times of crisis, or will they recognize Turkey as a constitutive, transformative and strategic actor in the reconstruction of the European security architecture? The real strategic meaning of the Ankara Summit lies in this question.

extraction.body: The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. A new agreement with Middle East powers demonstrates just how Turkey is acquiring the ability to organize other states around its own security relationships. September 21, 2026 - Nikola Lunić - Articles and Commentary Turkey is not leaving NATO. The harder question is whether the Alliance can accommodate a member that is simultaneously building a security architecture of its own. The defence agreement signed in Mecca on August 7th by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan initially looked like another regional arrangement produced by a Middle East in turmoil. Its implications may extend well beyond the three signatories. The agreement declares that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described the mechanism as technically similar to NATO’s Article 5, while stressing that it is not directed against Iran or any other country. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has indicated that the framework could expand, with Egypt among the possible future participants. The significance of the agreement lies in what it reveals about Turkey’s evolving approach to power. Ankara has spent years pursuing greater strategic autonomy while remaining a member of the western alliance system. The Mecca agreement suggests that Ankara may now be moving towards something more ambitious: strategic duality, in which Turkey stays inside NATO while building security relationships outside it in which it can act as a leading power. That possibility deserves closer attention in Europe. Turkey’s acquisition of the Russian S-400 air defence system offers an instructive precedent. The dispute which erupted between Ankara and Washington was connected to a weapons purchase that the US judged incompatible with NATO’s security architecture and risky for the F-35 programme. Turkey was removed from the F-35 programme and faced sanctions in retaliation. The episode demonstrated that NATO membership does not give Ankara unlimited freedom to build capabilities that conflict with core Allied interests. The Mecca agreement, however, raises a different kind of issue. The S-400 could be kept outside a procurement programme, with its deployment restricted and its interoperability denied. A security commitment is harder to unwind. Once institutionalized through ministerial consultations, military planning, intelligence cooperation and expectations of mutual support, such a commitment acquires political momentum on its own. The Mecca framework, though still deliberately flexible, is already moving in that direction. The question for NATO concerns the point at which external partnerships develop into a second collective-security framework. That distinction may not matter today. It could matter enormously in a future crisis. The Mecca agreement did not create a security network from nothing. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already concluded a strategic mutual-defence agreement in September 2025, under which aggression against one would be regarded as aggression against both. Turkey and Pakistan have spent years deepening a defence relationship covering industry, technology and counterterrorism. Turkey and Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, have moved towards closer economic and defence cooperation. Mecca institutionalizes these previously separate relationships within a trilateral framework that will include, according to the Turkish foreign minister, a ministerial committee and a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia. That detail is important as declarations of solidarity can be vague and fade over time. While institutions build continuity, create bureaucratic interests and shape expectations of their own. The three countries also bring complementary assets. Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, energy weight and a growing defence capability. Pakistan brings a large military, nuclear capability and decades of security cooperation with the Gulf states. Turkey contributes the most developed defence-industrial base of the three, a powerful conventional military, NATO membership and strategic geography. The combination does not amount to an alternative to NATO. Instead, it allows Ankara an opportunity to become the organizing power of a security network that exists outside the NATO alliance. Religion provides the narrative. Security provides the substance. The religious dimension of the agreement should be neither exaggerated nor ignored. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia share a common Islamic political vocabulary, and the choice of Mecca as the venue carries real symbolic weight. Their cooperation also reflects interests in deterrence, defence cooperation, military technology, regional stability and reducing dependence on external security providers. Religion supplies political legitimacy while security interests supply the substance. Yet, treating the agreement simply as religious solidarity risks underestimating the institutional components. Thus, its durability will depend on whether these interests remain aligned when a real crisis arrives. The Mecca agreement’s significance will ultimately be tested by a crisis. Suppose Saudi Arabia or Pakistan invokes the collective defence mechanism. Would Turkey respond according to its own national assessment, or consult NATO allies first? What happens if Washington and Ankara read the same crisis differently? These questions grow more consequential as the framework becomes institutionalized. Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, has stressed that the agreement is not directed against Iran or any other country, and that the form of assistance would be worked out through consultations after an attack. This makes the arrangement less rigid than Article 5 in practice. Flexibility does not eliminate strategic consequences. Ambiguous commitments leave room for manoeuvre while also leaving uncertainty about how partners will act once their interests diverge. For NATO this is a question of alliance cohesion. The Alliance has spent decades building integrated command structures, common standards and procedures for collective decision-making. The Mecca framework has none of this yet, so its political commitment currently runs well ahead of its demonstrated military capacity. That gap may narrow. This emerging duality for Turkey deserves particular attention in Europe. It sits at the intersection of Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia. It remains one of NATO’s most important military powers and is central to the Alliance’s southeastern flank. At the same time, Turkey has developed a foreign-policy network extending well beyond the Euro-Atlantic space. Its defence industry has become a central instrument of that strategy. Turkish drones, naval systems, armoured vehicles and missiles have created durable relationships with countries that share different formal alliances, alongside political and security ties across the Middle East, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Western Balkans. The Western Balkans are particularly relevant. Turkey has built its deepest security ties in the region with Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo – formalised in 2024 through comprehensive military framework agreements and reinforced by Turkey’s naval presence in Albania – while its cooperation with Bosnia and Herzegovina, though real, remains comparatively limited to bilateral training plans and equipment sales. Its growing defence-industrial presence gives these relationships an additional dimension. The Mecca agreement, however, goes one step further by building institutionalised collective security alongside bilateral and issue-specific ties Turkey has developed over the past decade. This is important for Europe as Turkish influence already shapes European security beyond NATO’s formal structures. The Black Sea is one such example. The Western Balkans are another. Turkey’s regional role is therefore becoming harder to read through the old question of whether Ankara is “turning towards” or “away from” the West. Turkey’s policies increasingly operate across several security environments at the same time. From strategic autonomy to strategic architecture The debate about Turkish foreign policy has long centred on strategic autonomy: Ankara’s effort to widen its freedom of action by reducing dependence on any single outside power. The S-400 purchase was one expression of this approach. The Mecca agreement suggests something further. Turkey is acquiring the ability to organise other states around its own security relationships. That is the difference between strategic autonomy and strategic architecture. An autonomous state seeks room to manoeuvre. A state capable of building its own security architecture can create room to manoeuvre for others as well. This gives Ankara an additional strategic asset and potentially greater leverage inside NATO. Turkey does not need an alternative to the Alliance to benefit from a parallel network. NATO membership raises the value of the new architecture because Ankara can draw on the Alliance’s credibility and capabilities while leading a separate structure outside it. That is the key to Turkish strategic duality. The Mecca agreement also fits in a broader shift in international security, in which regional powers increasingly hedge across overlapping partnerships rather than rely on one framework. Saudi Arabia maintains its relationship with the United States while deepening ties with Pakistan and Turkey. Pakistan combines its relationship with China with Gulf partnerships. Turkey stays in NATO while building its own networks. India has little reason to answer the Turkish-Pakistani relationship with a formal counter-bloc. Its likelier response is to deepen existing ties with Israel and the UAE. The pattern points towards a more fluid system of overlapping security networks in which states seek redundancy. A state can remain embedded in one security system while building another. The question is how these systems interact when their commitments collide. NATO has little reason to stop Turkey from developing legitimate partnerships outside the Alliance. Stronger regional capabilities can contribute to burden-sharing. The problem begins if an external framework creates obligations that conflict with Alliance priorities. The Mecca agreement has not reached that point yet. And there is no evidence of integrated command, common forces, joint operational planning or automatic intervention. Its mechanisms remain limited and its members retain wide freedom of interpretation. NATO should nevertheless follow how the framework develops. Its consultation mechanisms, intelligence cooperation, interoperability and defence-industrial cooperation will be important indicators of whether the agreement develops into a more substantial security structure. Turkey presents a particular case for the Alliance: a member developing a security network beyond NATO while remaining deeply embedded in the Alliance itself. That does not make Turkey an adversary; just a more complicated ally. It would be incorrect to say that the Mecca agreement establishes an “Islamic NATO”. What it does reveal, however, is Turkey’s ability to operate inside and outside established security structures simultaneously. The agreement may still fail to become a durable collective-defence mechanism. Members may disagree over priorities, new participants may decline to join, and its procedures may remain deliberately vague. Therefore, what matters is that Ankara is acquiring an institutional platform to organize security relationships beyond the Alliance while remaining one of its most strategically important members. For Europe, the lesson is that the old assumption that a country must choose between western alignment and strategic independence is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Turkey may be able to pursue both. The S-400 dispute forced Washington to confront the limits of Turkish autonomy in the military-technical sphere. The Mecca agreement may eventually force NATO and its European members to confront those same limits in the political-security sphere. Nevertheless, Turkey is not leaving NATO. Thus, the harder question is whether NATO is prepared for a Turkey that increasingly has something of its own to lead outside it. Nikola Lunić is a Serbian geopolitical and security analyst and Navy Captain (Ret.). He previously served as Serbia’s Defence Attaché in London and Oslo and as Executive Director of the Council for Strategic Policy. He currently works as a Strategic Affairs Consultant and is a regular guest lecturer at the Faculty of Law, University of Osijek.

The Mecca agreement also fits in a broader shift in international security, in which regional powers increasingly hedge across overlapping partnerships rather than rely on one framework. Saudi Arabia maintains its relationship with the United States while deepening ties with Pakistan and Turkey. Pakistan combines its relationship with China with Gulf partnerships. Turkey stays in NATO while building its own networks. India has little reason to answer the Turkish-Pakistani relationship with a formal counter-bloc. Its likelier response is to deepen existing ties with Israel and the UAE.

The pattern points towards a more fluid system of overlapping security networks in which states seek redundancy. A state can remain embedded in one security system while building another. The question is how these systems interact when their commitments collide.

NATO has little reason to stop Turkey from developing legitimate partnerships outside the Alliance. Stronger regional capabilities can contribute to burden-sharing. The problem begins if an external framework creates obligations that conflict with Alliance priorities. The Mecca agreement has not reached that point yet. And there is no evidence of integrated command, common forces, joint operational planning or automatic intervention. Its mechanisms remain limited and its members retain wide freedom of interpretation. NATO should nevertheless follow how the framework develops. Its consultation mechanisms, intelligence cooperation, interoperability and defence-industrial cooperation will be important indicators of whether the agreement develops into a more substantial security structure.

Turkey presents a particular case for the Alliance: a member developing a security network beyond NATO while remaining deeply embedded in the Alliance itself. That does not make Turkey an adversary; just a more complicated ally.

It would be incorrect to say that the Mecca agreement establishes an “Islamic NATO”. What it does reveal, however, is Turkey’s ability to operate inside and outside established security structures simultaneously. The agreement may still fail to become a durable collective-defence mechanism. Members may disagree over priorities, new participants may decline to join, and its procedures may remain deliberately vague. Therefore, what matters is that Ankara is acquiring an institutional platform to organize security relationships beyond the Alliance while remaining one of its most strategically important members.

For Europe, the lesson is that the old assumption that a country must choose between western alignment and strategic independence is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Turkey may be able to pursue both. The S-400 dispute forced Washington to confront the limits of Turkish autonomy in the military-technical sphere. The Mecca agreement may eventually force NATO and its European members to confront those same limits in the political-security sphere.
Nevertheless, Turkey is not leaving NATO. Thus, the harder question is whether NATO is prepared for a Turkey that increasingly has something of its own to lead outside it.

He previously served as Serbia’s Defence Attaché in London and Oslo and as Executive Director of the Council for Strategic Policy. He currently works as a Strategic Affairs Consultant and is a regular guest lecturer at the Faculty of Law, University of Osijek.

passages: The LA Sparks announced plans to honor Hall of Fame center Lisa Leslie with a statue outside Crypto.com Arena.
She becomes just the second player in WNBA history to receive such recognition from a former franchise.
Lisa Leslie spent her entire 12-year career with the Sparks after joining the league at its 1997 inception.
The eight-time All-Star led LA to back-to-back championships in 2001 and 2002, earning three MVP awards and four Olympic gold medals during her playing career.
Lisa Leslie says Kobe Bryant ‘was really like a little brother’
"To be cemented in Los Angeles, the city that raised me, I couldn't be more proud," Leslie said in a team statement .
Lisa Leslie Calls Marina Mabrey a "Game-Changer" in the Latest 'Fast Friends'
Leslie holds the Sparks' all-time records in points, rebounds, blocks, field goals, free throws, minutes, and games.
Her eight First Team All-WNBA selections rank second all-time.
Lisa Leslie Talks Post-WNBA Success on '1v1 with Kelley O'Hara'
Sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany are behind the piece.
The ceremony takes place September 20th, before the Sparks host 2026 WNBA expansion side Portland.

"Lisa's legacy isn't just measured by championships and accolades," said Johnson. "She is a pioneer, a cultural icon, and a force who elevated women's basketball to new heights." Sculptors Julie Rotblatt Amrany and Omri Amrany are behind the piece. The ceremony takes place September 20th, before the Sparks host 2026 WNBA expansion side Portland. Leslie thanked fans for their support and recalled her interactions with them during a halftime speech at the Sparks' 105-84 victory over the Portland Fire on Sunday. “This game does not get to where we are today without all of you who have been here, sitting with us, riding with us,” Leslie said. “Every time I've been in this arena, I have never left this arena without signing autographs, taking pictures, and giving you guys my all. I left it out here on the floor because that's what you deserve as fans.” Leslie said she viewed every game as “a moment to change the mind of a man who was a hater. It was a chance to convince somebody who didn't believe in women's basketball. It was an opportunity to let a little girl believe that she could be me and my teammates out here because it's all about love and hope. “And at the end of the day, it's more than a sport. It's an opportunity to change people's lives. It's an opportunity to build community. It's an opportunity to bring people together. So if you don't remember anything about me, I thank God that I have a statue out there to remind you, but remember, it's always been about love and basketball.” Leslie became the 16th person and second female to be honored with a statue outside Crypto.com Arena. The other female is Gigi Bryant, who was killed along with her father, Kobe Bryant, in a 2020 helicopter crash. On September 17, the SEC announced a five-year conditional innovation exemption for qualifying blockchain-based trading venues. The order allows Tokenized Securities Venues to facilitate trading in certain National Market System stocks under specified conditions. It provides relief from certain Exchange Act exchange and dealer requirements and permits the use of permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools. The exemption is temporary and conditional rather than a permanent regulatory framework. Bitcoin witnessed a notable surge after the announcement and crossed the $80,000 mark on Friday . Market capitalization was listed at $1.633 trillion, with 24-hour trading volume of $35.698 billion. Circulating supply totaled 20.087 million BTC against a maximum supply of 21 million. Bitcoin’s all-time high of $126,080 was recorded on October 6, 2025. Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, stated that the order includes specific requirements . According to Thorn , a tokenized venue must verify that the token provides holders the same rights and privileges as traditional NMS stock of an equivalent class. For third-party wrappers, the order requires distribution or availability of related proxy materials and other issuer communications at no cost to the issuer or shareholders. In an X post on Saturday, Schiff argued that tokenized securities backed by profitable companies offer a superior store of value compared with Bitcoin (BTC) .

Schiff described the Bitcoin rally as disconnected from the substance of the SEC announcement. He said digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a more reliable store of value than a token backed by nothing.
Tokenized stocks, in his view, provide the conveniences associated with Bitcoin without the risk he associated with a decentralized structure that could collapse.

On September 17, the SEC announced a five-year conditional innovation exemption for qualifying blockchain-based trading venues. The order allows Tokenized Securities Venues to facilitate trading in certain National Market System stocks under specified conditions.

It provides relief from certain Exchange Act exchange and dealer requirements and permits the use of permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools. The exemption is temporary and conditional rather than a permanent regulatory framework.

Bitcoin witnessed a notable surge after the announcement and crossed the $80,000 mark on Friday . At the time of this writing (on September 19 at 2:00 pm UTC), the asset traded at $81,290.43 on Saturday, September 19, 2026, according to CoinGecko data, up 1.6 percent over the prior 24 hours.

Bitcoin’s 24-hour range was $79,925.66 to $81,674.72. Its seven-day range was $75,038.12 to $81,674.72. Market capitalization was listed at $1.633 trillion, with 24-hour trading volume of $35.698 billion. Circulating supply totaled 20.087 million BTC against a maximum supply of 21 million. Bitcoin’s all-time high of $126,080 was recorded on October 6, 2025.

Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, stated that the order includes specific requirements . According to Thorn , a tokenized venue must verify that the token provides holders the same rights and privileges as traditional NMS stock of an equivalent class.

For third-party wrappers, the order requires distribution or availability of related proxy materials and other issuer communications at no cost to the issuer or shareholders. Dividends, voting rights and proxy distribution are required under the text of the order, Thorn said.

Comments posted on the platform X addressed Schiff’s remarks, rejecting his theory. An X user, LinDawg, stated that Schiff does not have the mental capacity to understand the real value of Bitcoin and described him as a traditionalist unable to adapt to digital assets.

Another user, Mr. Plenty wrote that the current price level presents a good opportunity to short. The 20 Delta Guy said Bitcoin could move substantially higher and that Schiff has issued repeated warnings of declines that have not occurred, adding that he should move on.

Bitcoin critic Peter Schiff said Friday’s Bitcoin price increase following the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s tokenized stock announcement was illogical and bearish for the cryptocurrency . In an X post on Saturday, Schiff argued that tokenized securities backed by profitable companies offer a superior store of value compared with Bitcoin (BTC) . Yesterday’s big Bitcoin rally following the SEC’s tokenized stock announcement makes no sense. The news is actually bearish for Bitcoin, which must now compete with tokenized securities. Digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a superior,… Schiff described the Bitcoin rally as disconnected from the substance of the SEC announcement. He said digital ownership of tokens backed by profitable, dividend-paying companies is a more reliable store of value than a token backed by nothing. Tokenized stocks, in his view, provide the conveniences associated with Bitcoin without the risk he associated with a decentralized structure that could collapse. On September 17, the SEC announced a five-year conditional innovation exemption for qualifying blockchain-based trading venues. The order allows Tokenized Securities Venues to facilitate trading in certain National Market System stocks under specified conditions. It provides relief from certain Exchange Act exchange and dealer requirements and permits the use of permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools. The exemption is temporary and conditional rather than a permanent regulatory framework. Bitcoin witnessed a notable surge after the announcement and crossed the $80,000 mark on Friday . At the time of this writing (on September 19 at 2:00 pm UTC), the asset traded at $81,290.43 on Saturday, September 19, 2026, according to CoinGecko data, up 1.6 percent over the prior 24 hours. Bitcoin’s 24-hour range was $79,925.66 to $81,674.72. Its seven-day range was $75,038.12 to $81,674.72. Market capitalization was listed at $1.633 trillion, with 24-hour trading volume of $35.698 billion. Circulating supply totaled 20.087 million BTC against a maximum supply of 21 million. Bitcoin’s all-time high of $126,080 was recorded on October 6, 2025. Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, stated that the order includes specific requirements . According to Thorn , a tokenized venue must verify that the token provides holders the same rights and privileges as traditional NMS stock of an equivalent class. For third-party wrappers, the order requires distribution or availability of related proxy materials and other issuer communications at no cost to the issuer or shareholders. Dividends, voting rights and proxy distribution are required under the text of the order, Thorn said. Comments posted on the platform X addressed Schiff’s remarks, rejecting his theory. An X user, LinDawg, stated that Schiff does not have the mental capacity to understand the real value of Bitcoin and described him as a traditionalist unable to adapt to digital assets. Another user, Mr. Plenty wrote that the current price level presents a good opportunity to short. The 20 Delta Guy said Bitcoin could move substantially higher and that Schiff has issued repeated warnings of declines that have not occurred, adding that he should move on. Rabbi Nakamoto stated that Schiff is emotionally opposed to Bitcoin and that no amount of logical explanation would alter that position , wishing him a nice weekend. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Bitcoin's moves upward don't occur in a perfect march; it tends to follow a pattern more like two steps forward and then one step back. On that note, even after helping to spark the recent uptrend, spot Bitcoin ETFs posted $462.7 million in net outflows during the week ending Sept. 11, breaking a three-week net buying streak, perhaps due to fears that the Federal Reserve was going to hike interest rates in the following week. (Which, of course, it did.) The mechanism here is that the issuers of Bitcoin ETFs need to buy coins to back their ETF shares. U.S.-based ETFs absorbed about $3.8 billion in net inflows over the three weeks through Sept. 4, per SoSoValue data, including $730.8 million in inflows on Sept. 3 alone. However, those inflows can quickly turn to outflows if sentiment shifts. On Sept. 15, the day before the Federal Reserve's announcement of a 25-basis-point federal funds rate hike, there were $450.4 million in net outflows. Inflation is the second force driving demand for Bitcoin, and it's substantially stickier and longer-lasting than the ETF flows are. Most likely, at least some of the ETF inflows are actually being driven by investors seeking inflation-resistant assets due to fears of monetary debasement. That fear is fully understandable, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Sept. 11 that consumer prices rose 3.4% year over year in August. That was just the latest information suggesting that the U.S. dollar is continuing to lose purchasing power at an accelerated pace compared to before 2020. Investors expecting that pace to continue are logically moving their money into fixed-supply assets, and Bitcoin is one of the largest ones other than gold. The third force that's supporting higher Bitcoin prices is on-chain data on miner stress and capitulation, the point at which the pool of willing sellers is largely spent. In a research report, the asset manager VanEck found that eight of 12 holder capitulation signals were flashing as of Aug. 12; those signals include factors like average holding periods and liquidation rates of supply that hasn't moved in multiple years. One of those other indicators, mining difficulty, was 18.3% beneath its November 2025 peak. A decline that steep suggests that unprofitable miners decided to stop mining, and also that they likely sold some or most of their coins to cover their underwater costs. That squeeze is already easing. VanEck reported that the Aug. 8 adjustment raised difficulty by 1%, the first upward print of the sequence. Passing that turning point has historically led to the coin's price running higher for many months. Eventually, those indicators will lift out of their capitulation range. That shift would mark the distress ending rather than the rally, and inflation fears could keep supporting the price well after it happens. In other words, expect this rally to continue for now. That fear is fully understandable, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Sept. 11 that consumer prices rose 3.4% year over year in August. That was just the latest information suggesting that the U.S. dollar is continuing to lose purchasing power at an accelerated pace compared to before 2020. Investors expecting that pace to continue are logically moving their money into fixed-supply assets, and Bitcoin is one of the largest ones other than gold.
The third force that's supporting higher Bitcoin prices is on-chain data on miner stress and capitulation, the point at which the pool of willing sellers is largely spent.

In a research report, the asset manager VanEck found that eight of 12 holder capitulation signals were flashing as of Aug. 12; those signals include factors like average holding periods and liquidation rates of supply that hasn't moved in multiple years. One of those other indicators, mining difficulty, was 18.3% beneath its November 2025 peak.

A decline that steep suggests that unprofitable miners decided to stop mining, and also that they likely sold some or most of their coins to cover their underwater costs. That squeeze is already easing. VanEck reported that the Aug. 8 adjustment raised difficulty by 1%, the first upward print of the sequence. Passing that turning point has historically led to the coin's price running higher for many months.

Eventually, those indicators will lift out of their capitulation range. That shift would mark the distress ending rather than the rally, and inflation fears could keep supporting the price well after it happens.
In other words, expect this rally to continue for now.

The security breaches were more like blips — not unpredictable harbingers of a hive-minded “swarm” ready to take over the web. “The attack in no way represents some sort of rebellion by the AI models. . . . In fact, they did exactly what they were told to do. They were not given adequate guardrails or containment,” said Akhil Verghese, founder of Krazimo, an AI software company. “They were simply told to get the best result possible on a test, and they correctly identified that the best way to do that was to get the answers, which is what they proceeded to do.” Tales of AI anarchy are being used to concoct an AI-security crisis to cement a critical public-private partnership just months after the companies announced plans to become publicly traded companies, some observers believe. Two recent incidents have stoked the fear-mongering. In the first, Hugging Face , an open-source platform used to build and share AI models, made the shocking announcement July 16 that it had been hacked by AI agents who navigated and exploited vulnerabilities in the website’s code without any human supervision. Five days later, OpenAI announced its GPT-5.6 Sol model and another unreleased model were testing in a “sandbox” — a purportedly closed off internal testing ground — broke containment and hacked Hugging Face to find the answers to the test it was taking. “One man’s ‘the model escaped the sandbox’ is another man’s ‘you failed to build the sandbox correctly.’ There was a live route to the internet . . . and nobody was watching what the agents were doing while it ran,” said Abhi Kumar, co-founder of Voice AI. “The thing that set it off. . . was an agent handed a spreadsheet task it couldn’t finish, because the files sat behind links it couldn’t reach. So it went looking for a way out. That’s not a machine waking up. That’s an impossible task in a leaky box, and a system doing exactly what you built it to do.” Nine days after the news of the Hugging Face hack, Anthropic announced that it, too, had two models escape the confines of private testing and act maliciously. Claude Opus 4.7 found a real company online that was similar to the fictional company from the test and attacked the company believing it to be part of the exercise. The second model, Mythos 5, created a malicious software package and uploaded it to online marketplace Python Package Index, where it was downloaded 15 times. The incidents have been used as justification for the federal government to regulate the frontier AI labs . In his call to “Pace the Frontier,” Amodei wrote the Hugging Face incident was his second biggest concern, behind only the speed of advancement he claimed to have witnessed occur over the last summer. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails,” Amodei wrote in his blog post on Sept. 12. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) launched an investigation into OpenAI on Sept. 9 from the Homeland Security and Government Affairs subcommittee, giving the company until Oct. 1 to turn over internal records on the Hugging Face incident. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) announced he would be introducing a bill that would ban the further development of the frontier labs. “The leaders of the major AI companies publicly acknowledge that they do not fully understand the technology and that it is escaping their control,” he said. “It is irresponsible for society to allow them to move forward and make these products even more advanced.” Sen. Elizabeth Warren on Wednesday called for an immediate pause on progress: “Frontier AI models are currently a dangerous technology, without the safeguards needed to protect people from serious harm … And it means passing legislation to put stronger guardrails in place before we have a cyber attack, an economic crisis, or a national security disaster facilitated by AI.” But industry insiders say recent incidents reveal real gaps in AI safety — without justifying the doomsday warnings now coming from Capitol Hill. “What isn’t a real fear is the implication that these agents went rogue, broke their containment in some way that was completely unpredictable, and hacked into Hugging Face because they felt like doing it. They acted exactly as they were instructed to do,” said Verghese. “It feels exaggerated to say, the leap feels quite large, to go from you know ‘we didn’t build the right sort of box’ to ‘everyone should be extremely alarmed and everyone in government should jump on this topic,'” Taivo Pungas, chief intelligence officer at Pactum AI, told The Post.

extraction.body: New Designations Designed to Strengthen Leadership Structure to Advance Strategic Priorities and Execution DALLAS , Sept. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI ) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today announced an update to the leadership structure of its Board of Directors (the "Board"), designed to further align the Company's governance with its strategic direction and business priorities. Appointment of Jaymes Winters as Chairman & Chief Executive Officer Additionally, effective September 16, 2026, the Board has appointed Chief Executive Officer Jaymes Winters to also serve as Chairman of the Board, effective immediately. Mr. Winters will continue to serve as Chief Executive Officer, assuming the combined role of Chairman and CEO. Mr. Winters brings more than 15 years of experience as a Chief Executive across the oil and gas, telecommunications and retail sectors, with extensive experience in mergers and acquisitions. Prior to Solidion, he served as CEO of Nubia Brand International Corp, a Special Purpose Acquisition Company and previously founded and served as CEO of United Energy Inc., which grew to nearly $100m in revenue under his leadership. Mr. Winters directed and negotiated significant M&A transactions involving private equity firms and previously served for more than 9 years as an adjunct professor in the School of Business at Portland State University, where he taught business strategy, mergers and acquisitions and venture capital. He holds a B.S. in Business Administration with a minor in Economics from Oregon State University. "Solidion is entering an important stage in its development, and we believe this leadership structure provides the Company with the alignment and accountability necessary to execute on our strategic priorities," said Mark Schwartz, Lead Independent Director. The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”.

extraction.body: The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”. Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”. “2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.” Coxon’s remarks, which were backed by two other researchers at the maker of the AI system Claude, prompted an international debate about the dangers and lack of oversight of AI as companies race to develop ever more powerful models. US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents. Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, Sam Altman, the boss of the ChatGPT maker OpenAI, and Elon Musk have called for development of the technology to be slowed down. However, Donald Trump has dismissed anxiety over the AI development as a “hoax” and a “conspiracy” , adding that a slowdown could give China the edge. On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, said the US and China had agreed to set up an AI dialogue mechanism to alert each other to help contain the technology’s potential dangers. Huang said predictions of an extinction-level event caused by AI were “not grounded in science”. Huang also claimed AI companies’ recent calls for national and international safety regulation aim to duck existing laws that would hold them to account. Citing recent cases where AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI triggered cybersecurity incidents during testing, he said there were plenty of laws to tackle the problems. “You have cybersecurity unauthorised entry laws, you have damage liabilities … if your product does harm, if your product doesn’t perform as you promised, and if you entered into contracts with companies for service level agreements, there are plenty of laws associated with that. My point is, apply those first. And don’t let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.” He continued: “Now, go and read between the lines. They’re actually not asking for more laws. They’re asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that’s a problem.” On Monday the the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) thinktank published a paper arguing that countries risk “profound and compounding disadvantage” if they fail to embrace AI and fall behind other nations. However, it also warned that the institutions meant to support the choices leaders would have to make were not equipped to do so . “The previous [industrial] revolution transformed our world over generations, AI will do so within a decade,” said Tony Blair in a foreword to the paper . “New capabilities are emerging at an extraordinary pace, with profound implications for economies, education, science, labour markets, public services and national security. But the risks are equally profound and growing, and so too is public concern. “Today’s political leaders… must make hard choices that will signficantly alter their countries’ trajectories. However, the institutions of the modern state meant to support political leaders in making these choices are simply not equipped for what is coming.”

Gopass is a free, open-source password manager that stores credentials in an encrypted store and runs from the command line. Its maintainers built it as a drop-in replacement for pass, the standard Unix password manager. Out of the box, Gopass encrypts each secret with GPG and keeps the store in a git repository. Git gives a team a record of every change and a way to sync one store across laptops and servers. Users who want different tools can switch encryption to age, switch storage to fossil, or drop versioning with the --storage=fs flag. The tool needs no network connection unless the user wants one, so it also runs on an air-gapped machine, a computer kept off every network. Private keys never leave your machine. The encryption comes from GnuPG, so a store is only as safe as each user’s handling of their GPG key. The maintainers point users to Homebrew, MacPorts, Fedora, Arch Linux, Alpine Linux, WinGet, Chocolatey, Scoop, and the FreeBSD and OpenBSD ports. Fedora users may first need to enable the daftaupe/gopass Copr repository. The tool runs on Linux, macOS, Windows and the BSDs, and the maintainers aim for the same user experience on each.

extraction.body: This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale . At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence , so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems. But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.” To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities. That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me. Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out? No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic. In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building. Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario : If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention. extraction.body: You can now talk with ChatGPT, Claude and more while you're on the road. If you love using AI chatbots like ChatGPT on your phone, you'll be pleased to know that accessing them in your car is also easy — if you have a car with Apple CarPlay. That's thanks to an API that arrived with iOS 26.4 allowing developers to bring AI chatbots into CarPlay, with a few already available. You just need to make sure you have the latest versions of their apps installed. For safety while driving, AI tools compatible with CarPlay only work through voice commands. Most of them let you jump back into an existing conversation from another device, at least. Before you continue, make sure your iPhone is running iOS 26.4 or later by visiting Settings > General > Software Update . If an update is available, follow the steps to install it. After that, open the App Store, tap your profile icon at the top-right, choose App Updates , swipe down to refresh, then choose Update All to make sure you have the latest versions of installed AI apps. As the most popular AI bot, it's no surprise that ChatGPT is CarPlay-ready . If you already have it on your iPhone, you'll find it on your CarPlay Home Screen. If you don't have it yet, download ChatGPT for free from the App Store (the same goes for the other apps discussed). With your iPhone connected to your car, tap the ChatGPT icon on CarPlay and select New Voice Chat . Then speak naturally when the app indicates it's listening. If you're not a fan of ChatGPT, several other options are available. Perplexity is one, with Meta AI and xAI's Grok also supported. More recently, Anthropic's Claude has also joined the list of chatbots available on CarPlay. Plus, if you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27 , Siri AI is available too — though this requires an iPhone 15 Pro or later for Apple Intelligence. When you open any of the apps in CarPlay, start a new chat or pick up where you left off before (all with your voice). For Siri AI, try using the "Hey Siri" command if it's available in your car. You can ask about anything, like suggestions on what to do at your destination. If you're driving alone, these chatbots can be a fun way to keep you entertained.
